newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil farmers ditch cotton, rice for soybean.
newsitem.headline: Brazil farmers ditch cotton, rice for soybean.

text.p: Brazilian farmers are dumping cotton and rice cultivation to plant more soybean and take advantage of good international prices for the oilseed, Agriculture Minister Arlindo Porto said.

Porto, revealing the first estimates for the 1996/97 grains and oilseeds crop, said the amount of land planted with cotton was expected to fall between 29.6 percent and 24.6 percent in the next crop year and rice by 11.2 percent to 7.1 percent.
Soybean plantings should increase 3.1 percent to 6.6 percent, to between 10.43 million ha and 10.79 million ha in 1996/97 from 1995/96.
"We are seeing a high capitalization in the soybean sector," Porto said.
The estimates from the ministry's Agricultural Supply Company (CONAB) predict a national soybean crop next harvest of up to 25.91 million tonnes from an estimated 23.19 million tonnes in 1995/96.

CONAB estimated that Parana state would hold the title it won this year as Brazil's leading soybean state, with production seen at between 6.49 million tonnes and 6.68 million tonnes from 6.24 million tonnes in 1995/96.

Rio Grande do Sul, traditionally soybean king in Brazil until hit by a severe drought last year, was seen producing 5.69 million tonnes to 5.9 million tonnes in 1996/97 after 4.4 million tonnes this harvest.
Among other leading producer states, Mato Grosso was expected to harvest 4.75 million tonnes to 4.89 million tonnes, up from 4.69 million tonnes.
And Mato Grosso do Sul's production was seen little changed in the next harvest at between 2.05 million tonnes and 2.13 million tonnes.
"We are witnessing an increase in productivity due to good climactic condition," Porto told reporters.
